claim: The gold-standard univariate method for assessing circadian phase is based on collection of a 24-hr time series of plasma melatonin.
source: The gold-standard univariate method is based on collection of a 24-hr time series of plasma melatonin, a suprachiasmatic nucleus-driven pineal hormone.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established practice in the field.

claim: Plasma melatonin is a suprachiasmatic nucleus-driven pineal hormone.
source: The gold-standard univariate method is based on collection of a 24-hr time series of plasma melatonin, a suprachiasmatic nucleus-driven pineal hormone.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about melatonin.

claim: A multivariate whole-blood mRNA-based predictor of melatonin phase was developed and validated.
source: We developed and validated a multivariate whole-blood mRNA-based predictor of melatonin phase which requires few samples.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study as stated in the abstract.

claim: Transcriptome data were collected under normal, sleep-deprivation and abnormal sleep-timing conditions.
source: Transcriptome data were collected under normal, sleep-deprivation and abnormal sleep-timing conditions to assess robustness of the predictor.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Partial least square regression (PLSR) applied to the transcriptome identified a set of 100 biomarkers.
source: Partial least square regression (PLSR), applied to the transcriptome, identified a set of 100 biomarkers primarily related to glucocorticoid signaling and immune function.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: The 100 biomarkers identified by PLSR are primarily related to glucocorticoid signaling and immune function.
source: Partial least square regression (PLSR), applied to the transcriptome, identified a set of 100 biomarkers primarily related to glucocorticoid signaling and immune function.
evidence: This is a finding from functional analysis of the identified biomarkers.

claim: PLSR-based predictors outperform published blood-derived circadian phase predictors.
source: Validation showed that PLSR-based predictors outperform published blood-derived circadian phase predictors.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the validation analysis.

claim: When given one sample as input, the R2 of predicted vs observed phase was 0.74 for the PLSR-based predictor.
source: When given one sample as input, the R2 of predicted vs observed phase was 0.74, whereas for two samples taken 12 hr apart, R2 was 0.90.
evidence: This is a quantitative performance metric from the validation analysis.

claim: For two samples taken 12 hr apart, the R2 of predicted vs observed phase was 0.90 for the PLSR-based predictor.
source: When given one sample as input, the R2 of predicted vs observed phase was 0.74, whereas for two samples taken 12 hr apart, R2 was 0.90.
evidence: This is a quantitative performance metric from the validation analysis.

claim: Many physiological and molecular variables exhibit 24 hr rhythmicity generated by central and peripheral circadian oscillators, as well as environmental and behavioral influences.
source: Many physiological and molecular variables exhibit 24 hr rhythmicity generated by central and peripheral circadian oscillators, as well as environmental and behavioral influences (Morris et al., 2012; Mohawk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The master circadian pacemaker is located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus.
source: The master circadian pacemaker located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus drives 24 hr rhythmicity in endocrine and neural factors such as cortisol, melatonin and the autonomic nervous system (Brancaccio et al., 2014; Kalsbeek and Fliers, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The SCN drives 24 hr rhythmicity in endocrine and neural factors such as cortisol, melatonin and the autonomic nervous system.
source: The master circadian pacemaker located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus drives 24 hr rhythmicity in endocrine and neural factors such as cortisol, melatonin and the autonomic nervous system (Brancaccio et al., 2014; Kalsbeek and Fliers, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Under normal conditions, the SCN is synchronized to the 24 hr light-dark (L-D) cycle by a light-input pathway.
source: Under normal conditions, the SCN is synchronized to the 24 hr light-dark (L-D) cycle by a light-input pathway (Lucas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The effects of light on the SCN depend on the timing, that is, the circadian phase of the SCN, at which light is administered.
source: The effects of light on the SCN depend on the timing, that is, the circadian phase of the SCN, at which light is administered (St Hilaire et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The SCN is sensitive to feedback from the pineal melatonin rhythm which impinges on the SCN through its melatonin receptors.
source: The SCN is also sensitive to feedback from the pineal melatonin rhythm which impinges on the SCN through its melatonin receptors (Pevet and Challet, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Exogenous melatonin can phase-shift and entrain the SCN, but its effects depend on the circadian phase of melatonin administration.
source: Exogenous melatonin can phase-shift and entrain the SCN, but its effects depend on the circadian phase of melatonin administration (Lewy et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Synchronization of the SCN to the L-D cycle and synchronization of the sleep-wake cycle to the SCN are disrupted during shift work and jet lag and in circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders (CRSWDs).
source: Synchronization of the SCN to the L-D cycle and synchronization of the sleep-wake cycle to the SCN are disrupted during shift work and jet lag and in circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders (CRSWDs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about circadian disruption.

claim: Delayed sleep-wake phase disorder is prevalent in adolescents.
source: Examples of CRSWDs are delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, which is prevalent in adolescents (Micic et al., 2016), and non-24-hr sleep-wake disorder, such as occurs in blind individuals (Sack et al., 1992; Sack and Lewy, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Non-24-hr sleep-wake disorder occurs in blind individuals.
source: Examples of CRSWDs are delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, which is prevalent in adolescents (Micic et al., 2016), and non-24-hr sleep-wake disorder, such as occurs in blind individuals (Sack et al., 1992; Sack and Lewy, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Treatment of circadian disorders by melatonin or light exploits the circadian phase-dependent response of the SCN to these stimuli.
source: Treatment of these circadian disorders by melatonin or light exploits the circadian phase-dependent response of the SCN to these stimuli (Auger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Optimal treatment of circadian disorders requires that the circadian phase of the SCN is known.
source: Optimal treatment requires that the circadian phase of the SCN is known and is thereby one example of chronotherapy, an increasingly important field in drug development and medicine (Dallmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a logical requirement for treatment, supported by a citation.

claim: Knowledge of the circadian phase of the SCN is informative for the diagnosis of CRSWDs.
source: Knowledge of the circadian phase of the SCN is also informative for the diagnosis of CRSWDs, assessment of adaptation to new time zones, adaptation to shift work (Mullington et al., 2016) and identification of circadian rhythm disturbances in psychiatric conditions.
evidence: This is stated as an application of circadian phase knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: In human blood, 6.4–8.8% of the transcriptome exhibits circadian rhythmicity when sleep occurs in phase with the melatonin cycle and in the absence of a sleep-wake cycle.
source: In human blood, 6.4–8.8% of the transcriptome exhibits circadian rhythmicity when sleep occurs in phase with the melatonin cycle and in the absence of a sleep-wake cycle (Archer et al., 2014; Möller-Levet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: When sleep occurs out of phase with the melatonin rhythm, only 1% of transcripts are rhythmic.
source: This peripheral circadian rhythmicity is, however, markedly disrupted when sleep occurs out of phase with the melatonin rhythm. Under these conditions, only 1% of transcripts are rhythmic (Archer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The human blood transcriptome is affected by both chronic sleep restriction and acute total sleep deprivation.
source: The human blood transcriptome is also affected by both chronic sleep restriction and acute total sleep deprivation (Möller-Levet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: mRNA abundance features and melatonin concentrations were assessed in blood samples collected under four sleep timing conditions.
source: mRNA abundance features and melatonin concentrations were assessed in blood samples collected under four sleep timing conditions (Archer et al., 2014; Möller-Levet et al., 2013) (Figure 1d,h): (i) Sleep in phase with melatonin; (ii) Sleep out of phase with melatonin; (iii) total sleep deprivation, no prior sleep debt and (iv) total sleep deprivation, with prior sleep debt.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and data collection.

claim: The melatonin rhythm persists in the absence of sleep and when sleep occurs during the daytime provided that light levels are low.
source: The melatonin rhythm persists in the absence of sleep and when sleep occurs during the daytime provided that light levels are low, as was the case in these experiments (Figure 1d,h).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Each of 678 genome-wide mRNA abundance profiles were assigned a circadian melatonin phase by referencing it to the onset of melatonin secretion (0 degrees) in the corresponding individual time series.
source: Each of 678 genome-wide mRNA abundance profiles were assigned a circadian melatonin phase by referencing it to the onset of melatonin secretion (0 degrees) in the corresponding individual time series (Archer et al., 2014; Möller-Levet et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the methodology for phase assignment.

claim: The data set was divided into a training set comprising 329 samples and a validation set comprising 349 samples.
source: To develop practical models, we divided our data set into a training set comprising 329 samples and a validation set comprising 349 samples (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the data partitioning for model development.

claim: Overall 24 hr rhythmicity in the transcriptome is most prominent in the 'sleep in phase with melatonin' condition.
source: Plotting the r2 value against the rank of the correlation shows that overall 24 hr rhythmicity in the transcriptome is most prominent in the 'sleep in phase with melatonin' condition and smallest in the 'sleep out of phase with melatonin' condition (Figure 2a,d).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Overall 24 hr rhythmicity in the transcriptome is smallest in the 'sleep out of phase with melatonin' condition.
source: Plotting the r2 value against the rank of the correlation shows that overall 24 hr rhythmicity in the transcriptome is most prominent in the 'sleep in phase with melatonin' condition and smallest in the 'sleep out of phase with melatonin' condition (Figure 2a,d).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Seventy-three features satisfied the criterion of a minimum correlation of 0.3 in each condition and across all four conditions for the molecular timetable method.
source: Seventy-three features satisfied the criterion of a minimum correlation of 0.3 in each condition and across all four conditions (see Materials and methods and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for threshold derivation; Figure 2—figure supplement 2 for temporal profiles of genes comprising the timetable model derived from our data).
evidence: This is a result from the molecular timetable analysis.

claim: The 73 features identified for the molecular timetable model are associated with T cell receptor V(D)J recombination, somatic diversification of T cell receptor genes and somatic recombination of T cell receptor gene segments.
source: Gene ontology (GO) functional enrichment analysis of the 73 features showed that they were significantly (Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted p-value<0.05) associated with the following biological processes: T cell receptor V(D)J recombination, somatic diversification of T cell receptor genes and somatic recombination of T cell receptor gene segments (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from functional enrichment analysis.

claim: The molecular timetable model using 73 features predicts the circadian phase of samples in the validation set on average within 9 min of the observed melatonin phase.
source: The timetable model using these 73 features identified in the training set predicts the circadian phase of samples in the validation set on average within 9 min of the observed melatonin phase which is comparable to the 15 min and −2 min bias when the original gene lists of (Lech et al., 2016) and (Hughey et al., 2016) were used, respectively (Table 1, Figure 3c,f,i).
evidence: This is a performance metric from the validation analysis.

claim: The Zeitzeiger method identified 107 features as the optimal number with which to predict the circadian phase of one sample.
source: Our implementation of Zeitzeiger identified 107 features as the optimal number with which to predict the circadian phase of one sample (see Materials and methods and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the Zeitzeiger analysis.

claim: Only three genes, PER1, NR1D1 and NR1D2, from the original Zeitzeiger gene list identified in animal tissues were also identified as predictors when applied to human blood transcriptome data.
source: Only three genes, PER1, NR1D1 and NR1D2, from the original Zeitzeiger gene list identified in animal tissues (Hughey et al., 2016) were also identified as predictors when applied to our human blood transcriptome data.
evidence: This is a comparison result between the original Zeitzeiger and the current study.

claim: The 107 features identified by the Zeitzeiger model did not show any significant functional GO enrichment.
source: The 107 features identified by the Zeitzeiger model did not show any significant functional GO enrichment (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from functional enrichment analysis.

claim: For the one-sample PLSR model, the optimal parameters were a combination of five latent factors and 100 mRNA abundance features.
source: For predictions based on one blood sample, the optimal PLSR model parameters were a combination of five latent factors and 100 mRNA abundance features (see Figure 3—figure supplement 4a and b and Materials and methods; see Supplementary file 1C for the list of features and Supplementary file 1B for the list of 80 corresponding genes).
evidence: This is a result from the PLSR model optimization.

claim: Latent factor 1 of the one-sample PLSR model gives greatest weight to features significantly enriched for biological processes linked to immune and inflammatory response.
source: Latent factor 1, the factor that has the greatest covariation of x and y, gives greatest weight to features significantly enriched for biological processes linked to immune and inflammatory response (e.g. TCF7, LEF1, NFAM1, TFE3, GIMAP5, PRKCA, GAB2, CD28), muscle hypertrophy and cytokine production (e.g. IL13RA1, IL11RA, CCR7, IL1RAP, IL6ST).
evidence: This is a result from functional enrichment analysis of latent factors.

claim: Latent factor 4 of the one-sample PLSR model is enriched for circadian rhythm genes.
source: Latent factor 4: circadian rhythm (most significant enrichment and includes TIMELESS, ID2, PROK2, GHRL, PER1, PER2, PER3), response to estrogen (CITED4, GHRL, SOCS1, SOCS3, BGLAP, LDLR, IL1B, DUSP1), response to growth hormone (IRS2, GHRL, SOCS1, SOCS3) and response to corticosteroid stimulus (ANXA3, IL1RN, IL1B, BGLAP, DUSP1, SOCS3).
evidence: This is a result from functional enrichment analysis of latent factors.

claim: Latent factor 4 contains the temperature-sensitive RNA binding proteins CIRBP and RBM3, which are known to regulate the translation of circadian transcripts.
source: In addition to being enriched for genes involved in circadian rhythmicity, latent factor 4 also contains the temperature-sensitive RNA binding proteins CIRBP and RBM3, which are known to regulate the translation of circadian transcripts (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis, with the function of CIRBP and RBM3 supported by a citation.

claim: Functional enrichment analysis of the 80 genes targeted by the 100 mRNA abundance features identified significantly enriched biological processes associated with leukocyte activation and inflammatory response.
source: Functional enrichment analysis of the 80 genes targeted by the 100 mRNA abundance features identified significantly enriched biological processes associated with leukocyte activation (HSPH1, SH2D1B, IL6ST, CCND3, CD1C, NCR1, TNFSF4, FLT3, IL1B, TXK) and inflammatory response (TLR2, TNFSF4, GHRL, IL1B).
evidence: This is a result from functional enrichment analysis.

claim: The one-sample PLSR-based model outperformed all other models for most performance metrics.
source: The one-sample PLSR-based model outperformed all other models discussed so far, for most performance metrics (Table 1, Figure 3).
evidence: This is a comparative result from the validation analysis.

claim: Fifty-four percent of samples fell within ≤2 hr of the true circadian phase for the one-sample PLSR model.
source: Fifty-four percent of samples fell within ≤2 hr of the true circadian phase and the R2 of 0.74 also compares well to other models.
evidence: This is a performance metric from the validation analysis.

claim: The prediction error of the one-sample PLSR model did not differ significantly across the four conditions.
source: Finally, the prediction error of the one-sample PLSR model did not differ significantly across the four conditions.
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of model performance.

claim: Two-samples performed better than one-sample, and three-samples performed better than two for the one-sample models applied to consecutive samples.
source: We thus applied the one-sample models to pairs and triplets of consecutive samples. Two-samples performed better than one-sample, and three-samples performed better than two (Table 1, Figure 3j,k and l, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a comparative result from the validation analysis.

claim: The PLSR-based model gave the best performance with 71% of samples having a prediction error of ≤2 hr and a R2 of 0.88 using three consecutive samples.
source: The PLSR-based model gave the best performance with 71% of samples having a prediction error of ≤2 hr and a R2 of 0.88 using three consecutive samples.
evidence: This is a performance metric from the validation analysis.

claim: When taking three consecutive samples as input, the model performed significantly worse for samples derived from the condition 'sleeping out of phase with melatonin'.
source: However, when taking three consecutive samples as input, the model performed significantly worse for samples derived from the condition 'sleeping out of phase with melatonin' (Tukey HSD post-hoc test, p-value<0.05).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of model performance across conditions.

claim: The trained two-sample differential PLSR model comprises 5 latent factors and 100 features.
source: Our trained two-sample differential PLSR model comprises 5 latent factors and 100 features (see Supplementary file 1D for the list of features and Supplementary file 1B for the list of corresponding genes).
evidence: This describes the structure of the two-sample differential PLSR model.

claim: For the two-sample differential PLSR, four of the five latent factors contained genes enriched for circadian rhythm or rhythmic process.
source: For the two-sample differential PLSR, four of the five latent factors contained genes enriched for circadian rhythm or rhythmic process.
evidence: This is a result from functional enrichment analysis of latent factors.

claim: Latent factor 2 of the two-sample differential PLSR model contained six clock genes (ARNTL, NR1D1, NR1D2, PER1, PER2, PER3) together with CIRBP and RBM3.
source: Each factor contained at least three clock genes, with factor two containing six genes (ARNTL, NR1D1, NR1D2, PER1, PER2, PER3) together with CIRBP and RBM3.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of latent factors.

claim: Forty-seven (62%) of the 76 unique genes targeted by the features identified using the two-sample approach also appear in the set of 80 unique genes identified by the one-sample approach.
source: Forty-seven (62%) of the 76 unique genes targeted by the features identified using the two-sample approach also appear in the set of 80 unique genes identified by our one-sample approach (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a comparison result between the two PLSR models.

claim: Both two-sample differential models outperform their preceding one-sample models and multiple consecutive-sample applications.
source: Both two-sample differential models outperform their preceding one-sample models and multiple consecutive-sample applications (Figure 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 5, Table 1).
evidence: This is a comparative result from the validation analysis.

claim: The two-sample differential PLSR model is able to predict within 20 min on average, with an SD of 1 hr 41 min.
source: The PLSR-based model performs well, now able to predict within 20 min on average, with an SD of 1 hr 41 min, without any significant difference in error distribution across circadian phase bins.
evidence: This is a performance metric from the validation analysis.

claim: The two-sample differential PLSR model is able to correctly predict 82% of samples within 2 hr, with an R2 of 0.9.
source: Significantly, the two-sample differential model is able to correctly predict 82% of samples within 2 hr, with an R2 of 0.9.
evidence: This is a performance metric from the validation analysis.

claim: The two-sample differential model has a significant difference in error distribution between conditions, where 'Sleep out of phase with melatonin' has a significantly larger mean error than the other three conditions.
source: However, unlike the one-sample PLSR model, we find a significant difference in error distribution between conditions, where 'Sleep out of phase with melatonin' has a significantly larger mean error than the other three conditions (Tukey-HSD post-hoc test p-value<0.05).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of model performance across conditions.

claim: A few transcriptome samples contain enough information to predict the phase of the melatonin rhythm even under conditions in which the sleep-wake cycle is desynchronized from the melatonin rhythm.
source: The analyses presented here show that a few transcriptome samples contain enough information to predict the phase of the melatonin rhythm. This remains true even under conditions in which the sleep-wake cycle, which also influences the blood transcriptome, is desynchronized from the melatonin rhythm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Melatonin phase and shifts in melatonin phase correlate well with other variables driven by the SCN, for example, cortisol.
source: Melatonin phase and shifts in melatonin phase correlate well with other variables driven by the SCN, for example, cortisol (Dijk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In clinical practice, it is assumed that the melatonin phase reflects the status of the SCN with minimal error.
source: In clinical practice, it is therefore assumed that the melatonin phase reflects the status of the SCN with minimal error, although the actual error in SCN phase measurement by melatonin is not known.
evidence: This is stated as current clinical practice.

claim: The PLSR-based approach is the first method for developing a melatonin phase predictor without a priori selection of features or feature characteristics.
source: We consider our PLSR-based approach the first method for developing a melatonin phase predictor without a priori selection of features or feature characteristics: no a priori information is used to supervise model development.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the approach.

claim: The PLSR-based model comprising features selected a posteriori outperforms 'a priori' approaches.
source: The validation analyses show that our model comprising features selected a posteriori outperforms 'a priori' approaches.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the comparative validation analysis.

claim: Many of the genes identified by PLSR are not classical clock genes or clock-controlled genes.
source: It should be noted that many of the genes identified by PLSR are not classical clock genes or clock-controlled genes (see Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of identified genes.

claim: 68% of the genes forming the one-sample PLSR-based model were previously identified as being rhythmically expressed in at least one of the four conditions analyzed.
source: Nevertheless, 68% of the genes forming the one-sample, and 63% genes forming the two-sample differential PLSR-based model, we have previously identified as being rhythmically expressed in at least one of the four conditions we have analyzed (Archer et al., 2014; Möller-Levet et al., 2013; Laing et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous findings from the same research group.

claim: 63% of genes forming the two-sample differential PLSR-based model were previously identified as being rhythmically expressed in at least one of the four conditions analyzed.
source: Nevertheless, 68% of the genes forming the one-sample, and 63% genes forming the two-sample differential PLSR-based model, we have previously identified as being rhythmically expressed in at least one of the four conditions we have analyzed (Archer et al., 2014; Möller-Levet et al., 2013; Laing et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous findings from the same research group.

claim: More than 30% of the gene lists forming the PLSR-based models are unique to the approach compared to the molecular timetable and Zeitzeiger approaches.
source: However, comparing across prediction models it is clear that >30% (34% and 31% for the one-sample and two-sample differential models, respectively) of the gene lists forming the PLSR-based models are unique to the approach (compared to the molecular timetable and Zeitzeiger approaches applied to the same training data set) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a comparison result between different modeling approaches.

claim: Six genes were identified in all four models: PER1, SMAP2, DDIT4, NCR1, ZBTB16 and FKBP5.
source: Six genes were identified in all four models: PER1 (circadian clock gene, induced by glucocorticoid [Cuesta et al., 2015]), SMAP2 (involved in vesicle trafficking in the trans-golgi network [Funaki et al., 2013]), DDIT4 (part of mTOR signaling pathway [Polman et al., 2012]), NCR1 (natural killer cell receptor [Lai and Mager, 2012]), ZBTB16 (transcription factor that regulates glucocorticoid-induced gene expression [Wasim et al., 2010]) and FKBP5 (chaperone that plays a key role in the regulation of glucocorticoid receptor signaling [Binder, 2009]).
evidence: This is a result from comparing gene lists across models, with functions supported by citations.

claim: Apart from SMAP2 and NCR1, all genes identified in all four models are involved in glucocorticoid signaling or are regulated by glucocorticoid.
source: Apart from SMAP2 and NCR1, all these genes are involved in glucocorticoid signaling or are regulated by glucocorticoid.
evidence: This is an inference from the functional analysis of the common genes.

claim: Immune function and glucocorticoid signaling are themes that link all four models.
source: Immune function and glucocorticoid signaling are themes that link all four models.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the functional analysis of genes across models.

claim: More than one third of all the genes in the four models are associated with glucocorticoid signaling.
source: More than one third of all the genes in the four models are associated with glucocorticoid signaling (molecular timetable 44%, Zeitzeiger 36%, one-sample PLSR 36%, two-sample differential PLSR 38%) (Nehmé et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from functional analysis, supported by a citation.

claim: The gene lists of the molecular timetable and Zeitzeiger models show little overlap with those of the PLSR models, which have a high level of similarity (62%).
source: The gene lists of the molecular timetable and Zeitzeiger models show little overlap with those of the PLSR models, which have a high level of similarity (62%).
evidence: This is a comparison result between different modeling approaches.

claim: Fifteen of the top-25 genes (by weighting) in the PLSR gene lists are common to both one-sample and two-sample differential models.
source: Fifteen of the top-25 genes (by weighting) in the PLSR gene lists are common to both models (PER1, DDIT4, FKBP5, ZNF397, TSPAN4, C20orf112, MIA, AVIL, ZBTB16, SPATA6, A_24_P178167, BQ706262, SMAP2, FLT3, HSPH1).
evidence: This is a comparison result between the two PLSR models.

claim: Twelve of the genes in the top-25 lists are associated with glucocorticoid signaling and form part of a linked glucocorticoid signaling network.
source: Twelve of the genes in the top-25 lists are associated with glucocorticoid signaling and form part of a linked glucocorticoid signaling network (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from functional analysis and network analysis.

claim: The top four features in the PLSR two-sample differential model gene list are present in all four models (DDIT4, PER1, FKBP5 and ZBTB16).
source: The top four features in the PLSR two-sample differential model gene list are present in all four models (DDIT4, PER1, FKBP5 and ZBTB16).
evidence: This is a comparison result across all models.

claim: Only the feature lists identified by the two sample differential PSLR model appear enriched for rhythmic, circadian processes.
source: Only the feature lists identified by the two sample differential PSLR model appear enriched for rhythmic, circadian processes.
evidence: This is a result from functional enrichment analysis.

claim: In the differential two-sample approach individual differences in average levels of expression (i.e. trait like characteristics of the transcriptome) are removed.
source: This may be because in the differential two-sample approach individual differences in average levels of expression (i.e. trait like characteristics of the transcriptome [De Boever et al., 2014]) are removed.
evidence: This is an inference about why the two-sample differential model shows enrichment for rhythmic processes, supported by a citation.

claim: Both the cortisol and the melatonin rhythm are driven by the SCN.
source: Both the cortisol and the melatonin rhythm are driven by the SCN.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The prominence of glucocorticoid signaling in the lists may reflect a more extensive influence of cortisol on the peripheral transcriptome.
source: The prominence of glucocorticoid signaling in the lists may reflect a more extensive influence of cortisol on the peripheral transcriptome.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The features of the PLSR models seem to focus more on genes with functions specifically related to blood such as glucocorticoid signaling and immune cell-specific roles.
source: Overall the features of the PLSR models seem to focus more on genes with functions specifically related to blood such as glucocorticoid signaling and immune cell-specific roles.
evidence: This is an observation from the functional analysis of identified genes.

claim: The influence of the sleep-wake cycle and circadian rhythmicity varies across the transcriptome transcripts in blood.
source: We have previously shown that the influence of the sleep-wake cycle and circadian rhythmicity varies across the transcriptome transcripts in blood (Archer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Whether and how blood-cell-specific functions remain in phase with the SCN, even when the sleep-wake cycle is shifted, remains unclear.
source: Thus, the features within the blood transcriptome that are most predictive of the melatonin phase are closely related to blood-cell-specific functions. We have previously shown that the influence of the sleep-wake cycle and circadian rhythmicity varies across the transcriptome transcripts in blood (Archer et al., 2014). Whether and how these blood-cell-specific functions remain in phase with the SCN, even when the sleep-wake cycle is shifted, remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as an open question based on the findings.

claim: The enhanced power of PLSR-based models compared to others cannot be due to the unique combination of experimental conditions because all models were tested on the same data sets.
source: The enhanced power of our PLSR-based models compared to others cannot be due to the unique combination of experimental conditions that we have included in our training and validation sets because all models were tested on the same data sets.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the source of model performance differences.

claim: All samples were collected in darkness and dim light and from young healthy individuals.
source: Our training and validation data are limited; all samples were collected in darkness and dim light and from young healthy individuals.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the study's data.

claim: Inclusion of conditions in which synchrony between various organs is challenged is important for model validation.
source: Comparing the performance of the various models across conditions emphasizes the importance of inclusion of conditions in which synchrony between various organs is challenged.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis across conditions.

claim: Several models that performed well under normal conditions performed less well under desynchronized conditions.
source: Several models that performed well under normal conditions performed less well under desynchronized conditions.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparative analysis across conditions.

claim: The conditional dependency of performance for the two-sample differential models is expected to be due to the significant temporal disruption evoked by sleeping out of phase with melatonin.
source: Indeed, we expect the conditional dependency of performance for the two-sample differential models to be due to the significant temporal disruption evoked by sleeping out of phase with melatonin, where the difference in mRNA abundance between two samples taken 12 hr apart may not be so well preserved as in baseline and/or sleep deprivation conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed performance differences.

claim: In the Dim-Light-Melatonin Onset (DLMO) Protocol, many samples (6–18) are collected during an approximately 6–12 hr period timed to be close to the expected onset of melatonin secretion.
